newsitem.title: UK: British government cuts clone scientists' funds.
newsitem.headline: British government cuts clone scientists' funds.

text.p: Britain's Agriculture Ministry has decided to cut funding for the institute in Scotland that produced the world's first adult cloned animal, the scientists who did the controversial research said on Saturday.

Although they doubted the decision was due to the international furore that arose over the birth of Dolly the cloned sheep, scientists at the Roslin Institute warned that they and their research could be forced into the arms of purely commercial interests.

"We had the formal letter on February 27," said Grahame Bulfield, director of the institute. "At the moment 65 percent of the work in Ian Wilmut's lab is supported by MAFF (the Ministry of Agriculture, Fisheries and Food)," he added, referring to the scientist who led the cloning research. "It's a major problem."

Government ministers, newspapers and even prominent scientists such as Nobel Peace Prize winner Joseph Rotblat have raised the spectre of mad scientists using the Roslin technology to create carbon copies of dictators, film stars or millionaires.

Bulfield denies this is likely and repudiates the idea of cloning people. But he said the funding cuts could drive the Institute away from "pure" science and its original brief, which was to make advances in animal breeding for farms.
He said the cuts would affect several projects, including 50 percent of the "Dolly" cloning programme this year and 100 percent of the government funding for the programme starting on April 1, 1998.

"The package is over 600,000 pounds ($976,000) out of a total of 3.5 million, which is just under 20 percent," he told Reuters in a telephone interview. He said half the institute's funding came from outside contracts and half from the government.

The Roslin Institute has a close partnership with biotechnology company PPL Therapeutics Plc, which holds licences for some of the work being done there - the genetic engineering of animals to produce human proteins for use in medicines.
It also has working arrangements with other pharmaceutical companies. Bulfield warned that cutting government funding could force the scientists to dance entirely to the tune of commercial interests.

"If we can't get funding from anywhere else...my job is to keep the institute going," he said. He said he had received "thousands of calls" from the United States, where the interest in genetic engineering and cloning research is strong.
"If it is a matter of redundancies (lost jobs) versus U.S. corporate funding there is no doubt where my duty lies," he said.
"We have to be driven by wherever our customers want to drive us, whether those customers are government or industry," he said. "We live in a real world. "
Bulfield said he had been getting hints of cuts since November, so he doubted the government was reacting to this week's alarming front-page headlines.
"It's the cock-up theory. It was some cranky decision made by some junior member of the policy area," he complained. "It's not a plan at all."
The British scientists say the cloning technique opens up great possibilities, for instance in research on ageing.
Bulfield said animal breeders who came to see Dolly this week were also keen.

"They all said it can't be used immediately but it's absolutely essential that we keep this work going because of the intellectual property involved and the ability of the UK to lead in this area," Bulfield said. ($ = 0.614 British Pounds)
